1.note: Read as The Hague: Italian L'Aia, Spanish La Haya, in Hebrew letters. Part 7 ends with the journey "from Amsterdam to האיוא", and below (paragraph 108) the Ḥida also calls the city האג, "Hague".

2.he: מוהר"ר שאול סג"ל גיסו של הגאון מוהר"ש מאמשטרדם שיש לו אחותו בת הגאון מוהר"ר ליב
2.note: Probably Saul ha-Levi, rabbi of the Ashkenazi community of The Hague; the "gaon R. S. of Amsterdam" is probably Saul Lowenstamm, chief rabbi of the Ashkenazim of Amsterdam, son of Aryeh Leib Lowenstamm ("the gaon R. Leib"), his predecessor there. The identifications are probable, not certain.

3.he: שינתה. בחרוז מח' לכ' ... והשיבה היא וקוי ה' יחליפו כ"ח
3.note: In the Ashkenazi pronunciation ḥet and kaf sound alike, so she rhymed a word ending in ח with one ending in כ. Her brother objected; she answered with Isa 40:31, "they that wait upon the Lord shall renew [literally: exchange] their strength (כח)", which the printing marks as letters: "shall exchange kaf-ḥet". The pun is the point of the story.

4.note: Probably Tobias Boas (about 1696–1782), the leading Jewish banker of The Hague, financier to the House of Orange; his sons continued the bank.

5.note: היסט is a small rabbinic measure, apparently the spread of the hand between thumb and forefinger; so the scroll was about two such spans tall. Sense uncertain.

6.note: Abraham Gabbai, the Ḥida's attendant on this journey, named in full in paragraph 111 and in part 7; not his son Abraham, who was then in Tunis.

7.note: Italian gabinetto, "cabinet". The Prince is William V of Orange, stadtholder; his Cabinet of Natural History and Rarities in The Hague was opened to visitors in these years (and was carried off to Paris in 1795).

8.note: Spanish agua fuerte (Italian acqua forte), "strong water": properly nitric acid, but here clearly the preserving spirit in which specimens were kept in jars.

9.note: Literally "the likeness of twelve litrin"; read as a weight of about twelve pounds (Latin libra, Italian libbra).

10.note: Perhaps Spanish toneles, "barrels", for the Dutch ton (gouds), "a ton of gold", a money of account of 100,000 guilders. Uncertain.

11.note: China, Italian Cina (ג' for the ch-sound). This reading also suits כתיבות הגינ"א in part 5 (note 9), the palm-leaf book in the Paris library.

12.he: וכמה סידורי עצים עם דמות הקן של כל אחד
12.note: Literally "several arrangements of trees (or wood) with the likeness of the nest of each one": probably birds' nests shown on branches, each with its bird. Sense uncertain.

13.note: The visit is in the full text: A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 82, 18 Elul [5536, 1776]: with Meir Trieste the Ḥida saw the room of the University of Padua where medical degrees were conferred, with minerals in cases, written labels, animals and the skeleton of a whale. The Livorno editors left it out. The collection is the natural-history museum of Vallisneri at the Palazzo del Bo.

14.note: Tuesday of the week of Beha'alotekha was 14 Sivan, 9 June 1778, the day of the visit to Baron Suasso (paragraph 103); the entries are not in strict order. The date follows the weekday and portion.

15.note: פ"ק is read as פרוטה קטנה, "even a small coin": not a penny. A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34) has the same phrase several times ("ולא נתנו לי אפילו פ"ק").

16.he: ר' משה לענן ור' שמעון זימיר
16.note: Printed לענן; A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34) reads לערן, Lehren, the name of a known family of Amsterdam. He names Simeon Zimir as a cantor (ר' שמעון זימיר החזן).

17.note: Read as the number ל"י = 40, printed without the marks; זהובים, "gold pieces", is the usual Hebrew for florins (guilders). Uncertain.

18.note: A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 160, reads הפליגו לכבד, "they went out of their way to honor me"; the 1885 "speaking" also fits the contrast with the winter, when no one spoke to him.

19.he: ר' משה שפריגר ... הרויח בלונט י"ב אלפים
19.note: שפריגר read as Springer. A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 160, prints בלו"ט, "in the lot(to)": the lottery (compare the lottery money in paragraph 106). The currency of the twelve thousand is not stated.

20.note: Read as "the 6th of Tammuz", like "יום כ"ו סיון" in paragraph 108, not as "Friday in Tammuz". The place of departure is not stated; the last place named is Rotterdam.

21.he: על המלכה שתתעבר וזה ד' חדשים שנתעברה
21.note: Marie Antoinette, childless after eight years of marriage. Her first child, Marie-Thérèse, was born on 19 December 1778, so by early July 1778 she was about three months pregnant. The first visit to Paris was in December 1777 and January 1778 (parts 4 and 5).

22.note: So printed (checked on the scan). Read as רי"ד, R. Isaiah di Trani, whose notes on the Pentateuch the Ḥida began to copy in the same library in January 1778 (part 5); ד and ר are easily confused. A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 163, prints ריי"ד.

23.note: So printed (checked on the scan); לנועה is not a word. Read as צנועה, "modest" (ל for צ is a common confusion in this type).

24.note: Samuel Peixotto, a Sephardi banker of Bordeaux, whose attempt to divorce his wife against her will became a lawsuit before the Parlement of Paris in 1778–1779, with printed briefs on both sides about Jewish divorce law. Abraham Gradis (part 4) was the leading Jewish merchant of Bordeaux.

25.note: Printed ומשה אבוקאטו שלו, "and Moses his advocate"; A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 164, reads ועשה אבוקאטו שלו ספר טענות, "and his advocate made a book of arguments": the advocate is not named, and "Moses" is a misreading of ועשה.

26.note: So printed (checked on the scan). Read as בעלילת, "by the plot of", or as בעצת, "on the advice of" (ל for צ, as in note 22).

27.note: Liefmann Calmer (1711–1784), a German-born Jew naturalized in France, who bought the barony of Picquigny and the vidamé of Amiens. As lord he held the right to present priests to church livings, which caused a scandal; "professor" may stand for French propriétaire or patron, "owner of an abomination" (a church benefice). Or it may mean that he professes a hateful doctrine. Sense uncertain.

28.he: ונלוה עמהם רבא מבורדיאוס והוא פק"ר. ר"ת פיגוט"ו קלמי"ר רב"א
28.note: Raba is a family name of the Sephardi merchants of Bordeaux, not "a rabbi". פקר (hefker, "lawless, heretical") is made of the initials פ-ק-ר of the three names; below, Amsterdam, London, Bordeaux give א-ל-ב, read as אבל ("mourning"), as the printing marks it.

29.note: The two quoted words are marked as abbreviations or numbers in the printing (מקל"י = 180, דוא"ג = 14 by gematria); a hidden reference may be intended and is not resolved. The plain sense: I passed over it with my staff alone (with restraint), when the slanderer (Doeg) came.

30.note: Signor Ariani is David Ḥayyim Ariani, the Ḥida's travelling companion (D. Ḥ. A. in part 5); so the index of A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34). The physician Monsieur Rast is not identified.

31.note: So the 1885 printing (כ' = 20); A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 169, reads כמו ד' שאלות, "about four questions".
